articles.title: Apple Photos AI watermark can tag your real pictures
articles.excerpt: Apple Photos now embeds an invisible SynthID watermark in images edited with Apple Intelligence tools like Clean Up, Extend and…
articles.fullText:
You take a great family photo, but there's one problem. Someone you don't know walked into the background. So you open Apple Photos , use Clean Up to remove the person and save your picture. Problem solved, right? Well, there's something new happening behind the scenes.
With iOS 27.2, Apple Photos can now add an invisible AI watermark to pictures you edit using certain Apple Intelligence tools . You won't see it on your screen. And if you share the photo, the person receiving it probably won't notice anything different either. But the watermark could still be there.
Apple introduced the feature in its Oct. 26 update. It uses Google's SynthID technology to identify images created or modified with artificial intelligence. Even a photo you took yourself can receive this hidden marker after certain AI edits. So how does it work, and what does it mean for the photos you share?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES
AI photo editing has come a long way. What once required complicated software can now take a few taps on your phone. That's convenient when you want to improve a picture. However, it also makes it harder to tell what's real. Someone can remove an important detail from a photo without leaving an obvious trace. AI can even generate parts of a scene that the camera never captured.
Apple's new watermarking feature gives people a way to tell when AI has been used to create or change an image. According to Apple's official support documentation, certain Apple Intelligence tools now add a hidden SynthID watermark when you create or edit images.
SynthID is technology developed by Google . It embeds a digital signal into an image that compatible detection tools can recognize. The watermark doesn't visibly change your photo. There's no stamp across the bottom or warning in the corner. Instead, the marker remains hidden unless someone checks the image with a SynthID detector.
Apple says the feature applies to certain Apple Intelligence tools starting with iOS 27.2. Here's where you might encounter it.
Clean Up lets you erase distractions from your pictures. Maybe someone wandered into your vacation photo. Or perhaps there's an object in the background you wish you could remove. You can use Clean Up to erase that distraction while AI fills in the missing area. With iOS 27.2, some photos edited this way can receive a SynthID watermark. However, Apple doesn't say that every small edit will trigger one. The watermark can depend on the changes made to the image.
Have you ever taken a picture and realized you were standing too close? Apple's Extend tool can help by generating additional scenery beyond the original edges of your photo. For example, you might have cropped out part of a building. Extend can generate additional background to make the composition look better. The result may look like you captured a wider shot in the first place. However, because AI creates part of the finished image, the photo can receive a hidden SynthID watermark. We've previously explained how Extend works in our article on fixing badly framed photos after you take them.
Apple also includes Spatial Reframing, called Reframe in Photos, among the tools covered by SynthID. Reframe lets you change the apparent perspective of a picture after you've taken it. You can adjust the angle or shift the composition while Apple Intelligence generates the necessary visual information. That can make a photo look quite different from what your camera originally captured. And because AI helps create that result, the edited image may carry a watermark.
Apple's watermarking feature also covers images generated using Image Playground and Image Wand . Image Playground lets you create images with AI using descriptions or other visual inputs. Image Wand can turn a rough sketch into a more developed image. Since these tools generate visual content, their inclusion makes sense. But Apple's decision to mark certain edits to genuine photos raises a more interesting question. Should a real photo receive an AI marker because you removed one distracting object?
NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS
You might be wondering whether there's an easy way to see if a photo contains one of these hidden markers. There is, although you'll need to use an online detector. Apple recommends Google's SynthID Detector, which can analyze an uploaded image for the watermark.
One thing to understand: finding a watermark doesn't automatically mean a photo is fake. It simply indicates that AI was involved in creating or modifying the image. And the reverse is also true. If no watermark appears, that doesn't prove the picture is genuine. Other AI image generators may not use SynthID. Detection can also have limitations. I would also be careful about uploading private family pictures or sensitive images to any online service. Review how the service handles uploaded files before submitting them.
Apple says photos created or edited before the 27.2 update won't automatically receive a new SynthID watermark from Apple. So you don't have to worry about the update going through your entire photo library and adding markers to everything.
However, that changes if you open an older picture and edit it using one of the supported AI tools. For example, you could take a photo from five years ago and use Extend to improve the framing today. The newly edited version may then receive the invisible watermark.
Apple has also expanded this feature beyond iPhones. According to the company, SynthID support begins with these software versions: iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 and visionOS 27.2. Keep in mind that the software update and Apple Intelligence have different device requirements.
OPENAI CHILD SAFETY TOOLS TARGET AI-GENERATED ABUSE
You'll need an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone to use the editing features that trigger these watermarks. Apple Intelligence works on the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, along with iPhone 16 models and newer compatible iPhones. The standard iPhone 15 can install iOS 27.2, but it doesn't support these Apple Intelligence editing features. Availability may also depend on your region and language.
To check for the latest software update:
I like the idea of giving people another way to question what they're seeing online. But there's an important limitation. Let's say you use Clean Up to remove someone standing behind your family in a vacation photo. Now compare that with an AI-generated picture showing an event that never happened. Both images could carry SynthID watermarks, even though the circumstances are very different.
The detector may identify AI involvement. However, it won't necessarily explain what was changed or how significant those changes were. That's a pretty big limitation when you're trying to decide whether to trust an image.
There's also the issue of AI-generated pictures that have no detectable watermark. So, while SynthID can provide a useful clue, it shouldn't be your only way of evaluating a suspicious photo. If a picture online seems questionable, look for the original source. You can also use a reverse image search to see where a photo originally appeared and whether earlier versions exist.
I can see why Apple is doing this. AI has gotten so good at changing photos that it's becoming harder to know what you're actually looking at. And I think that's a real concern. At the same time, I like having tools that can fix a great picture when someone walks into the background. Why should that photo get the same kind of watermark as a picture created entirely by AI? That's where I think Apple could do better. I'd love to see a way to check a photo and find out exactly what AI changed. Was it something minor, or did someone completely alter what happened? That's what I'd want to know before deciding whether to trust what I'm seeing.
Should Apple put a hidden AI watermark on your personal photos simply because you removed something from the background? Or should these markers be reserved for images that AI creates entirely? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Trump, Xi, Putin meeting was a spectacle that yielded little progress: analysts
articles.excerpt: Leaders discussed nuclear tensions, U.S.-China rivalry over AI and Taiwan’s status, but status quo remains.
articles.fullText:
Updated on Nov. 20, 2026 at 12:48 a.m. ET
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia concluded their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, but their meeting was more about “optics over substance,” experts told Radio Free Asia.
U.S. President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, describing the gathering as a historic diplomatic occasion.
Nuclear arms control and regional conflicts were high on the agenda amid deepening geopolitical and technological competition among the world’s major powers.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in his opening remarks.
Although the meeting may have been historic, the three leaders have national interests that do not quite align on the nuclear question, David Fedor, a Stephenson Policy Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, told RFA.
“Other than President Trump’s comments before the meetings about nuclear weapons, ... there was little signaling ahead of time that substantive decisions would be made,” said Fedor.
Xi called for the prohibition and destruction of nuclear weapons and the establishment of a world free of them, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The summit marked the first leader-level talks on nuclear arms control since New START expired in February. Its lapse ended the last remaining bilateral nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow, raising concerns about an unrestricted arms race.
Trump Xi Putin trilateral in China
Trump has called for a new agreement that would bring Beijing into nuclear arms control negotiations. China, however, has long maintained that Washington and Moscow should substantially reduce their stockpiles before asking it to accept limitations on its comparatively smaller arsenal.
China is estimated to possess more than 600 nuclear warheads, while the United States and Russia hold more than 5,000 each.
“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard not to have them,” Trump said. “So it’s not an easy thing to do, give them up.”
Xi also proposed regular high-level exchanges and the creation of a crisis communication mechanism among the three powers to help manage tensions.
No concrete agreement on nuclear arms control was immediately announced following the summit.
The White House released a statement that said the three leaders “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.
(Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik via Reuters) The statement also said that the three countries would hold dialogues on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and minimizing nuclear risks.
Taiwan’s security concerns
Ahead of Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Taiwan’s government downplayed expectations that the island would feature prominently in discussions among the three leaders.
“From what we know, Taiwan is not the focus,” Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told a news briefing in Taipei.
Liang said the discussions were more likely to prioritize securing a ceasefire in Ukraine and addressing Iran’s nuclear program.
“Even if Taiwan is mentioned, it will be a relatively peripheral issue,” he said.
Liang also expressed doubts about whether the three leaders could reach substantive agreements given their competing interests and the limited time available for negotiations.
“The three parties want different things, and their priorities are also different,” he said.
Taiwan nevertheless featured in a separate bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi earlier on Thursday, their third face-to-face meeting this year.
Xi told Trump that Washington should “stick to doing the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid major setbacks in relations between the two countries, China’s official Xinhua News Agency reported.
According to Xinhua, Trump told Xi that the United States “does not support Taiwan independence.”
The White House had not released its own account of the bilateral meeting at the time of Xinhua’s report.
These statements, and others on Ukraine, seemed to be a repeat of previous statements, Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, told RFA.
" This whole series of meetings have been big on optics and small on deliverables," said Chong. “⁠⁠There were general declaratory statements but little visible substantive progress, at least on to the public. ... I suppose repeating the basic principles are better than nothing."
People pass a sign for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 17, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) During the trilateral summit, Xi also called on major powers to respect each other’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and core interests, warning against crossing red lines on sensitive issues.
Taiwan, which joined APEC in 1991 under the name Chinese Taipei, is represented at this year’s summit by Acer founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih, appointed by President Lai Ching-te to attend on his behalf.
The lack of substance in statements regarding Taiwan was likely an outcome Taipei was hoping for, William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group.
“On Taiwan, an issue where there is very little basis for bilateral consensus, they basically treated it as a formality — something they had to mention briefly as part of the routine agenda, and then move on,” said Yang. “I think, overall, when the two sides’ readouts came out yesterday, the immediate reaction from the Taiwan government was probably one of relief.”
Neither Xi’s nor Trump’s statement did much to change the status quo for Taiwan, he said.
“Basically, Taiwan made it through another Trump-Xi meeting without any rhetoric being put forward that would cause major harm to Taiwan.”
Competition over artificial intelligence
The summit took place against a backdrop of mounting technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, particularly over artificial intelligence (AI) and access to advanced semiconductors.
Trump has held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips used to develop AI models, indicating that additional measures could aggravate bilateral tensions.
Xi urged Washington and Moscow to work with Beijing to maintain stable global supply chains and called on the three powers to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains.”
Competition over emerging technologies has become a major point of friction between the world’s two largest economies, alongside disagreements over trade and access to strategically important raw materials.
China's President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026.
(Doug Mills/AFP) U.S. officials have accused Beijing of failing to fully implement commitments made during a Trump-Xi meeting last year, including pledges to purchase more American agricultural products and ease export restrictions on rare earth minerals used in electronics manufacturing.
A trade truce reached last year following successive tariff increases is due to expire on Jan. 10, 2027, adding another source of uncertainty to bilateral relations.
The meeting between Xi and Trump did little to ease this uncertainty, Riley Walters, deputy director of the Japan Chair at the Washington-based Hudson Institute, told RFA.
“It sounds like Trump and U.S. officials are still waiting on China to buy more soybeans and export more rocks, meaning maybe no progress is being made since their last meeting,” said Riley.
“Instead, it sounds like Trump and Xi simply meeting and talking has become the baseline for this relationship, and so long as they continue meeting then it’s construction.”
Fedor said that Trump seems to feel a sense of responsibility in managing relationships with Xi and Putin.
That sentiment is what drives him to ”stage these very public interactions with leaders like Chairman Xi and President Putin," he said.
“But I do not think those visits substantively change the underlying interests of the relevant parties, at least some of which are fundamentally contradictory.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.
Update adds comments from experts.

articles.title: Could caviar served on gourmet food tour of North Korea violate UN sanctions?
articles.excerpt: Russian tour company offers a tour of high-end Pyongyang restaurants inaccessible to average North Koreans.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Caviar, wine, and foie gras served to Russian tourists in high-end Pyongyang restaurants is not necessarily evidence that exporters are violating sanctions that prohibit luxury items shipments to North Korea, but in the spirit of the sanctions these should be considered luxury items, a former member of the U.N. sanctions committee told Radio Free Asia.
Russian travel agency Vostok Intur is offering a gourmet tour that includes meals at many of the places frequented by North Korean elites: the twin-tower Koryo Hotel; the iconic Okryu-gwan restaurant, ground zero for Pyongyang’s high-class food culture; and a cruise ship sailing down the Taedong River which runs through the city.
The Russian Union of Travel Industry reported Monday that the travel company had completed its first gourmet tour with each participant paying roughly US$2,000 for the experience. The tour package includes an itinerary visiting restaurants inaccessible on standard tours, Inna Mukhina, the director of the travel agency, said in the report. The tour route and the restaurants are approved by North Korean tourism authorities, and it includes a stop at a restaurant called Rungra, where caviar and foie gras is served.
A table setting at a high-end Pyongyang restaurant, released by Vostok Intour, a travel agency based in Vladivostok, Russia.
(Vostok Intur) But whether this is a violation of sanctions depends on the interpretation of U.N. resolution 1718 – adopted by the U.N. Security Council in 2006 as a means to prevent the flow of cash and resources into North Korea’s nuclear missile programs. The resolution lists 14 luxury items that are banned for sale to North Korea, but caviar and foie gras are not among them.
The sanctions document should be viewed broadly rather than narrowly, Shuji Sue, a former member of the U.N. Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions, told RFA Tuesday.
“Because the luxury goods are not specifically exemplified, this has always been a subject of debate when the panel of experts drafts reports,” he said. “I reiterate that I view caviar as a luxury item and consider it to be a luxury product prohibited by the Security Council.”
The European Union designates caviar and its substitutes as prohibited luxury goods, and the U.K., Japan, and Singapore also ban the export of caviar to North Korea. Wine is also subject to the luxury goods export ban by the E.U., the U.S., and the U.K.
Vostok Intur plans to regularize gourmet tourism starting in 2027, once a month with a maximum of 10 people per trip. According to the itinerary released on the agency’s website, tourists will visit the Koryo Hotel restaurant, the Hwasong Kumgang restaurant at the top of the Pyongyang Clock Tower, the Taedong River floating restaurant, and Okryu-gwan.
The price of next year’s group tour package announced by the travel agency is approximately US$1,100, which includes a basic cost of 45,000 rubles (about US$550) plus US$550 for local accommodation expenses. Meal costs are calculated separately.
Even if the sanctions resolution is interpreted broadly, the caviar would not be a violation if it were produced domestically. RFA asked Vostok Intur about the source of the ingredients, but they did not respond.
Domestic production?
Though the source of the caviar has not been confirmed, North Korea has been farming sturgeon since the reign of Kim Jong Il, the father and predecessor of current leader Kim Jong Un. The state-run Korean Central News Agency reported in 2013 that the younger Kim visited a fish farm in South Hwanghae province, and said that his father’s last order before he died in 2011 was to raise as many sturgeon as possible so they could be prepared and served at Okryu-gwan.
This undated picture released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency on Feb. 21, 2017 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un visiting the Samchon catfish farm in South Hwanghae Province, North Korea.
(KCNA via AFP) RFA was not able to confirm whether North Korea produces caviar domestically, but if it does, it can only be in small quantities, Lee Hyunseung, a former member of the North Korean elite whose family fled North Korea in 2014 and who now resides in the United States, told RFA.
“We cannot confirm the exact production volume, but as long as fish farms exist, domestic production is possible,” said Lee, who works as a senior researcher at the Maryland-based Global Peace Foundation. “However, mass production is not feasible. Clearly, if the number of tourists increases and tourism programs are operated more frequently, imports would be necessary to guarantee the required quantity.”
China is the world’s largest producer and exporter of sturgeon caviar but Beijing’s official export statistics show no record of the delicacy being sent to North Korea between 2018 and 2025. Russia, meanwhile, has not disclosed bilateral trade statistics since 2022, meaning that potentially Chinese caviar could enter North Korea via Russia.
Inequality exposed
The gourmet food tours are a stark contrast to the lifestyles of the typical resident of North Korea, a country that struggles with chronic food shortages, where a month’s salary cannot even buy a bag of rice.
Lee said that restaurants such as the Koryo Hotel or the Taedong River cruise ship can cost up to hundreds of dollars for a single meal, making them inaccessible to most people living in North Korea.
RFA reported last month that an average factory worker earns 20,000 North Korean won, about 30 US cents at the market exchange rate.
According to Vostok Intur’s itineraries, the tourists’ lunches and dinners are ordered and paid for separately, with an average cost of US$20 per meal. This amount is equivalent to approximately five and a half times the average worker’s annual salary.
A group of Russian tourists arrive at the Pyongyang International Airport in Pyongyang, North Korea, Friday, Feb. 9, 2024.
(Cha Song Ho/AP) “ Russians travel to North Korea like this, pay US$2,000, and enjoy a luxurious trip for three nights and four days,” said Lee. “I wonder how many people in North Korea can actually afford to pay US$2,000 and enjoy that kind of luxury. Even the wealthy elites in the country simply cannot spend like that.”
According to South Korea’s Ministry of Unification, the cash-strapped North Korean government regards tourism as a key means of earning badly needed foreign currency.
“These tourism profits will also eventually be handed over to Kim Jong Un through the General Administration of National Tourism,” said Lee.
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: Cummins defiant amid fresh 'Sandpapergate' claims
articles.excerpt: Pat Cummins remained defiant on Thursday as his position as Australia Test captain was called into question after he was…
articles.fullText:
Pat Cummins remained defiant on Thursday as his position as Australia Test captain was called into question after he was dragged back into the "Sandpapergate" scandal by Cameron Bancroft's explosive revelations.

Bancroft, a central figure in the 2018 ball-tampering plot in South Africa that rocked world cricket, dropped a grenade late Wednesday in a lengthy newspaper column by claiming the whole team knew what was going on.

It came just days after Cummins held a 70-minute press conference to rebut the same allegations by Usman Khawaja in his autobiography, calling them "100 percent wrong".

Bancroft was the player who used sandpaper during a Test in Cape Town to make the ball swing, with a Cricket Australia probe concluding only he, then-skipper Steve Smith and his deputy David Warner were responsible.

They were all sent home in disgrace and banned.

In a statement to several Australian media outlets, Cummins' manager Neil Maxwell said: "Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one.

"Pat feels for Cam of course. He has been through a lot. We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said.

"Pat has rebuilt the Australian cricket team. That 24-year-old in Cape Town resolved to fix the team and spent eight years doing it," he added.

Despite the defiance, calls are mounting for his position to be reviewed.

"Pat Cummins' future as Test captain should be placed under immediate review after Cameron Bancroft's stunning accusation that the skipper didn't tell us the truth," The Australian newspaper said in an opinion piece.

"Cummins' press conference in Sydney last week when he forcefully denied any knowledge of the plot to use sandpaper in a Test in 2018 could become the worst strategic move of his career."

National broadcaster ABC agreed with the sentiment, saying "his position as captain of the Australian Test team is now questionable", while the Sydney Morning Herald stated: "Cummins' captaincy in peril".

The naming of Australia's squad for their home Test series against New Zealand in December-January was expected this week, but has now been pushed back.

Hours before Bancroft's revelations, Cricket Australia said it would not reopen its investigation but instead set up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018.

Chief executive Todd Greenberg also declared Cummins' version of events was not under scrutiny.

"No, the captain doesn't need to be cleared. No-one's looking to be cleared," Greenberg said.

Bancroft had suggested in a 2021 interview the bowling group, including Cummins, knew about the scheme.

In response, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly they were aware of the plan.

Starc reiterated his stance last week. Hazlewood and Lyon have yet to comment. Neither has Smith.

Bancroft said he felt "angry and betrayed" by Cummins' denials.

"It was not just the three of us. Steve Smith, David Warner and I knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," he wrote.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins's press conference."

In other revelations, Bancroft claimed Warner first raised the prospect of using sandpaper during the second Test at Port Elizabeth and coaches Darren Lehmann and David Saker were "certainly present" during talks about the issue.

Lehmann, who quit in the days after Cape Town, has continuously denied knowing anything.

Speaking on ABC radio during the third Australia-England one-dayer in Hobart on Wednesday, he said he would take time to work through Bancroft's allegations.

"It's only just come to light. I just need to sit back and process all that and work through each allegation," he said. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals semis with help from Tiafoe
articles.excerpt: Carlos Alcaraz reached the last four of the ATP Finals on Wednesday thanks to Frances Tiafoe after the Spaniard had…
articles.fullText:
Carlos Alcaraz reached the last four of the ATP Finals on Wednesday thanks to Frances Tiafoe after the Spaniard had earlier brushed aside world number five Daniil Medvedev 6-2, 6-4.

American Tiafoe beat Italian Flavio Cobolli 7-6 (8/6), 6-0 with his first set guaranteeing Alcaraz's spot in the next round.

Tiafoe kept his hopes of a semi-final spot alive in his maiden Finals appearance and faces Medvedev in his last group-stage match on Friday.

Seven-time Grand Slam champion Alcaraz needed just over 70 minutes to beat the Russian in Turin.

"A little bit of problems, you know, physically, in the match," Alcaraz said on-court after receiving some treatment in the second set.

"But I think everybody could see that I was able to still play good tennis, I could still move well."

By winning in straight sets, the 23-year-old will secure his spot in the semi-finals if Frances Tiafoe defeats Flavio Cobolli later or if the Italian beats the American in three sets.

Alcaraz has never won the season-ending Finals, finishing runner-up last year to Jannik Sinner.

But with Sinner injured and the Spaniard entering this season's edition on the back of a nine-match winning streak that earned him indoor titles in Vienna and at the Paris Masters, Alcaraz is considered the favourite to lift the trophy this year.

Since returning in August from a wrist injury that kept him off the tour for four months and prevented him from defending his French Open title, Alcaraz has won three of the five tournaments he has entered.

After easing past Tiafoe in his opener in Turin 6-2, 6-2, the third seed carried that ominous form into the first set against 2020 Finals winner Medvedev.

Alcaraz broke the Russian in successive games midway through the first frame to claim the opener.

He continued by breaking Medvedev in the very first game of the second set and proceeded to serve out, despite a brief stoppage to have his left thigh taped up.

"I didn't want to force myself to the limit physically. I was a break-up at that time. And I just tried to keep up my serve... play chill, smoothly, relaxed and just happy about it," Alcaraz said.

"So, I'm going to look at it with my team and I will see."

Medvedev, 30, is still in with a chance of advancing after winning his opening match against Cobolli in straight sets.

World number one Alexander Zverev is the man to beat in the John McEnroe Group and became the first player to book his spot in the semi-finals after beating Ben Shelton on Tuesday. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Fake vacation rental sites use live chat to steal your data
articles.excerpt: Fortra researchers say fake vacation rental sites use live customer support chats to trick travelers into handing over credit card…
articles.fullText:
You're booking a vacation rental for the holidays when a message appears saying there's a problem with your reservation. Before you can figure out what's wrong, a customer support chat opens and offers to help. You're told your credit card won't be charged, but you'll need to enter the number to complete a security check. Sounds helpful, right? That's exactly what scammers want you to think.
Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered fake vacation rental sites that look remarkably similar to legitimate booking platforms. Some even include live customer support chats designed to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. With Thanksgiving travel approaching, it's worth knowing how these scams work before you book your next trip.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
Researchers with Fortra's Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team recently identified fraudulent travel-booking websites that impersonate popular vacation rental platforms. The scammers copy legitimate property listings and surround them with details you'd expect to see on a real booking site. You might recognize the familiar layout or see reviews that make a property seem trustworthy. The photos may even come from an actual vacation rental.
One example uncovered by researchers showed listings for an apartment and a house. Both appeared to be legitimate properties available for booking. Someone searching for a holiday rental could easily spend more time comparing the accommodations than questioning the website itself. That's the problem. A professional-looking listing tells you very little about who's actually running the website. Fortra says its researchers identified and remediated examples of these phishing sites. The company did not report how many travelers may have fallen for the scams or whether money was stolen.
The scammers also know that travel plans can be stressful, especially around the holidays. If you've already arranged transportation and suddenly see a warning about your accommodations, you're probably going to want answers.
Researchers found fraudulent booking pages displaying messages such as:
In one case, a fake booking page told visitors their reservation was still unconfirmed. To finish the process, they needed to complete what the website called a mandatory verification step. The page reassured them that there would be no additional charge. But the next screen asked for personal information , including contact details that scammers could potentially use for future phishing attacks. Researchers also identified a separate website impersonating a major lodging platform. Its login page used recognizable branding and familiar sign-in options to encourage visitors to submit account information. That creates another risk. If you use the same password for multiple services, giving it to a fake booking website could put those other accounts in danger.
The live chat feature is what makes this scam particularly concerning. In a separate case, Fortra's researchers discovered a fraudulent travel-booking page with a credit card payment form and a live support chat. When visitors expressed concerns, the chat responded and described the card request as a routine security check. It even reassured visitors that their cards wouldn't be charged. Now consider how often you've used an online customer support chat to straighten out a billing problem. You explain what's happening, someone responds and you follow their instructions. Most of the time, that experience is perfectly legitimate.
Scammers are borrowing that familiar interaction to make their websites seem more trustworthy. The chat's reassurance was designed to encourage visitors to submit payment details . The researchers did not say whether a real person or an automated system operated the chat. Either way, the conversation was part of the fraudulent booking process. And that's an important reminder. Just because someone responds to your questions in real time doesn't mean you're dealing with the company you think you're dealing with.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL
Before you enter your credit card information or book a place to stay, take a moment to make sure you're dealing with a legitimate website. A little extra checking now could save you from losing money or having your personal information stolen.
If you're using Airbnb, Vrbo or another rental platform, open its official app or enter the website address yourself. Don't rely on links in unexpected emails or text messages, even when they mention a reservation you recognize. Be cautious with sponsored search results as well. Scammers sometimes pay for advertisements that lead to fraudulent websites . If you're unsure about a booking message, go back to your account through the official platform and look for it there.
A fake website may use a familiar company logo while hiding behind a completely unrelated web address. Scammers also add extra words to brand names to make fraudulent domains appear legitimate. Check the address before signing in or entering your credit card number. Remember that a padlock symbol doesn't guarantee a website is safe. It only indicates that the connection is encrypted.
Found a rental you really like? Search for the address separately and see whether the property appears on another reputable booking website. Compare the details and pay attention to prices that seem unusually low. You can also reverse-search the listing photos to see where else they're being used. However, finding matching photos doesn't automatically prove the listing is legitimate. Scammers often steal pictures from real properties. Take a few minutes to read reviews from previous guests. If something about the listing doesn't add up, contact the booking platform directly.
If a message claims your reservation will be canceled unless you act immediately, check your booking through the official website or app. A legitimate reservation problem may require attention, but that doesn't mean you should trust a link that arrived unexpectedly. If the warning doesn't appear in your account, contact customer support using the information published on the company's official website.
Be especially careful if a host asks you to visit another website to complete payment. The same goes for unexpected requests to move the conversation to WhatsApp or another messaging service. Airbnb warns that paying outside its platform can leave guests without AirCover protection. Vrbo also requires bookings and payments to follow its authorized process. Some legitimate properties may collect certain disclosed charges separately. If that happens, confirm the payment instructions through the official booking platform before sending money.
Strong antivirus software that includes malicious website and phishing protection can help warn you about known fraudulent booking pages. Some security programs can also detect suspicious links before you enter sensitive information. Keep your browser updated as well, since updates often include important security fixes. Of course, newly created scam websites may escape detection. Security software helps , but you still need to check where you're entering your information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Credit cards generally offer stronger protections for disputing fraudulent charges than many other payment methods. That's especially useful when you're paying for an expensive vacation rental. Be suspicious if someone insists on a wire transfer or wants payment through cryptocurrency. Gift card requests are another major warning sign. Once money is sent using these methods, recovering it can be difficult. Even when paying by credit card, make sure you're using the actual booking platform.
32 TRAVEL ESSENTIALS THAT HELP PROTECT YOU AND YOUR BELONGINGS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON
Some legitimate vacation rentals require identification. However, that doesn't mean you should upload your driver's license or other sensitive documents to an unfamiliar website. If you're asked to complete an unexpected verification process, confirm it through your official reservation. Also, never share a one-time security code with someone contacting you through a support chat or message. That code could give a scammer access to your account.
A password manager can help you recognize a suspicious login page. If the website address doesn't match the saved address for your account, the password manager generally won't autofill your credentials. That doesn't automatically prove the site is fraudulent, but it's a good reason to check the address more carefully. Use unique passwords for your booking accounts and enable two-factor authentication. Passkeys are another good option when a service supports them.
If you think you've shared personal or financial information with a scammer, act quickly. Here's what to do based on the information you provided.
I think the live chat feature makes this scam especially troubling. We're so used to turning to customer support when something goes wrong that we tend to trust the person offering to help. And that's exactly the reaction these scammers are hoping for. I wouldn't assume a booking website is legitimate simply because someone in a chat window tells me everything is fine. My advice? If you're asked to enter your credit card information to fix an unexpected reservation problem, stop and check with the booking company directly. I know that's frustrating when you're trying to get your holiday plans settled. But I'd rather spend a few extra minutes verifying a reservation than find out later that a scammer has my credit card number.
Have you ever had a vacation rental reservation suddenly require additional payment or verification? Did you trust the request, or did something make you suspicious? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Rohingya hope for justice as UN court prepares to rule on Myanmar genocide case
articles.excerpt: An activist who fled Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown says a historic ruling must lead to real change for refugees
articles.fullText:
A Rohingya activist who fled Myanmar as a teenager hopes a landmark ruling by the United Nations’ highest court on Thursday will bring long-awaited recognition of her community’s suffering, she told Radio Free Asia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is set to rule Nov. 19 on whether Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention during a military crackdown against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017, which forced more than 730,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh.
Though she hopes for a favorable ruling, Lucky Karim, a Rohingya who escaped the violence at the age of 14 and is now a human rights activist, warned that justice will mean little without action to protect refugees and allow them to return home.
“For Rohingya to have a positive outcome, it will be a historic moment, a historic victory for us,” she told RFA, adding that such a ruling could also offer hope to other ethnic minority communities in Myanmar, where years of conflict and military repression have displaced millions of people.
Lucky Karim, in front row on the left, with classmates at a primary school in Hlaing Thi village, Maungdaw Township, Rakhine State.
(Lucky Karim) Originally from Hlaing Thi village in Rakhine State’s Maungdaw township, Karim spent six years in a refugee camp in Bangladesh. In 2022, she founded Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, an organization advocating for the rights and education of Rohingya women.
Her hopes reflect the significance of a case that has taken seven years to reach a judgment and could establish Myanmar’s legal responsibility for one of the worst episodes of mass displacement in recent decades.
What happened to the Rohingya?
The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority from Myanmar’s western Rakhine State who have faced decades of discrimination, restrictions on movement and denial of citizenship in the Buddhist-majority country.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it described as clearance operations after Rohingya militants attacked security posts. Soldiers were accused of killing civilians, raping women and burning entire villages, driving hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.
A United Nations fact-finding mission later concluded that there were reasonable grounds to infer genocidal intent behind the military campaign and called for senior military officials to be investigated and prosecuted.
Myanmar has rejected accusations of genocide, maintaining that its operations were legitimate responses to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, a Rohingya insurgent group.
The Gambia, a small West African nation, brought the case against Myanmar in November 2019 with the backing of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
It accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention, an international treaty adopted after World War II that obliges countries to prevent and punish genocide.
A view of the Great Hall of Justice, the courtroom of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, June 18, 2026. (Nicolas Economou/Reuters)
(Reuters) The ICJ ordered Myanmar in January 2020 to take measures to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya and preserve evidence.
Myanmar’s government filed objections to the case in January 2021, just days before the country’s military took control of the country in a coup.
The court rejected the objections in 2022, and held hearings on the allegations in January this year.
During those hearings, The Gambia argued that the pattern of killings, sexual violence and destruction demonstrated an intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group. Myanmar’s military government disputed that interpretation, arguing that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold required to establish genocide.
What could the ruling change?
Thursday’s judgment will determine whether Myanmar bears responsibility under international law for violations of the Genocide Convention.
Unlike the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals, the ICJ settles disputes between countries. Its ruling cannot directly send military commanders to prison or compel the immediate return of refugees.
But a finding against Myanmar would carry legal and diplomatic weight and could require the country to take further measures to address violations and provide reparations.
For Karim, the distinction between a legal victory and improvements in refugees’ lives is crucial.
“The judgment from the International Court of Justice does not immediately change the ground reality. It doesn’t immediately repatriate refugees from refugee camps to Burma either,” she said, using Myanmar’s former name.
The challenges facing the Rohingya have only deepened since the 2017 crackdown.
After the 2021 coup, the country was plunged into a wider civil war. Renewed fighting in Rakhine State between the military and the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has exposed Rohingya civilians to further violence and displacement.
The United Nations said in May that approximately 150,000 Rohingya had arrived in Bangladesh since early 2024, adding to the pressure on already overcrowded refugee settlements.
Around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees were living in Bangladesh, according to the UN’s May estimate, most of them in and around Cox’s Bazar, home to one of the world’s largest refugee settlements.
Their return to Myanmar remains fraught with uncertainty, with concerns over safety, citizenship rights and protection from persecution still unresolved.
Lucky Karim is seen in front of the house where he lived in refugee camp number 8 in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, in March 2019.
(Lucky Karim) “Until it is safe for everyone, it’s not safe for any one of us in Burma,” Karim said.
She urged governments and international organizations to ensure that any judgment leads to concrete measures to protect refugees and create conditions for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.
The ICJ’s judgments are legally binding, although the court has no independent enforcement force. If a country fails to comply, the other party may seek action through the UN Security Council.
Karim said achieving lasting change would require sustained international commitment and the implementation of the court’s ruling, rather than simply recognizing the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
“So the judgment should not be a piece of paper,” she said. “It shouldn’t be another genocide declaration.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: AI data centers could consume more water than Americans drink in a year by 2030, says CEO working on solution
articles.excerpt: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says AI data centers could drink as much water as Americans by 2030 unless direct chip…
articles.fullText:
Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck, whose company is working on sustainable solutions to ecological problems like AI data centers ’ robust water consumption, said that without reform, AI data centers could wind up consuming more water than Americans drink every year.
"Ninety-five percent of the data centers today use a lot of water," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We estimate that by 2030, with the old technologies in the U.S., we will use as much water to cool data centers as Americans are using for drinking needs."
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
Beck argued that this phenomenon is "not sustainable," and laid out the technologies his company is working on in an effort to reduce data centers’ water consumption.
"Behind AI there's water in every step of the process. You need water to produce the chips, to power the chips and to cool the chips. And for the last four or five years, the chips generation that we were using were just cooled with air," he told Fox News Digital.
However, with the increasing complexity of chips to match an ever-building demand for computer power, air conditioning alone is no longer sufficient to cool chips in data centers, Beck explained.
"You need something that's way stronger. Water is 30 times better at extracting heat than air from the chips. So that's why many of those new data centers are moving toward direct chip water cooling, which ultimately is bringing cold water on top of the chip," he said.
Direct water cooling, he explained, has the dual benefits of increasing efficiency and sustainability, because the water used to cool the chips can be recycled and used on every chip in a given data center.
"So you end up in a place where you have a data center that is much more powerful [than] using no water, using less power, and ultimately not having an impact on natural resources and in communities around us, which is one of the unlocks that people are pushing back so much against right now," he said.
ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE
On Nov. 4, voters across the U.S. elected lawmakers and executives who ran on campaigns to limit the number of data centers.
In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa upset incumbent Republican Greg Abbott. Voters who ticked the box for Hinojosa did so after she campaigned heavily on instituting a data center moratorium , a fact that Beck took note of.
THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO
"Most of the data centers that were installed in Texas or anywhere else in the country or in the world, for that matter, were using a lot of water, a lot of power. And that's created a lot of backlash from the communities, which is rightfully so," Beck told Fox News Digital.
Beck noted that while Texas is one of the most economically strong states in the union, it is also one of the most water-stressed.
"It's a bad combination," he said. "Obviously, high growth, great news; no water, less good news. So we've looked at those technological solutions on how do you bring higher growth, more data processing while using much less water."
Beck added that the technologies Ecolab is developing will exclusively be used in new-build data centers, while the political pushback is surrounding the existing, more resource-demanding projects.
Direct cooling allows for what is known as a closed loop system , a method that is far more sustainable and requires less water than previous iterations of water-cooling methods.
Ecolab, Beck explained, has found a way to recycle water not only in the chip cooling process, but in chip fabrication as well, a process that necessitates extremely pure water.
"The so-called fabs, they use huge amounts of water, which is very specialized water because it needs to be ultra pure," Beck explained.
"And that, to be recycled, is even way harder than in a data center. But even there, at Ecolab we found solutions to not only get the highest purity of water to get the most advanced chips, but we can reuse that water as well in ways that are water neutral," he said.
Beck also put in context just how pure the water for chip fabrication needs to be.
"The purity is a million times more pure than what you would inject in your blood if it's a drug. So super high quality, super high purity of water at the end," he said.
"So the way we do it, in short, is ultimately at every step of the process we try to extract the water from that process step. We treat, we purify that water, we bring it back to an ultra-pure water level, and we bring back to the process. And the very special thing that we have at Ecolab, within that water you have some trace materials that we call connected water," he said.
"So we understand the quality of the water throughout the process within the fab or the data center, for that matter, that we know exactly the quality of that water to make sure that the chips are perfectly produced. And we know what we need to do in order to re-treat that water so that it can be reused afterwards. And you end up with better chips, lower cost, and most importantly, water neutral," Beck said.

articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit puts nuclear arms control, North Korea in focus
articles.excerpt: Analysts see little prospect of a nuclear deal, while Pyongyang hopes its allies will press its case with the US.
articles.fullText:
When U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold their first trilateral summit on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit , a concrete agreement on nuclear arms control would be an unlikely result, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
The meeting comes as Washington seeks to bring Beijing into nuclear discussions with Moscow, while China maintains that its smaller arsenal makes participation in such negotiations unreasonable. North Korea, meanwhile, is closely monitoring the meeting for any implications it might have for its own nuclear weapons program.
Though a deal is not likely, the summit could open channels for further consultations on nuclear risks, Cheng Xiaonong, a U.S.-based Chinese scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
“My understanding is that Trump is essentially trying to use Putin to teach Xi Jinping a lesson,” he said. “Of course, Putin will want to negotiate something in return.”
U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Iori Sagisawa/Reuters) Trump is scheduled to meet Xi bilaterally before joining Putin for trilateral talks. Discussions are expected to include nuclear disarmament or the wars in Ukraine and Iran, although China has not released a detailed agenda.
North Korea, which maintains close ties with both Beijing and Moscow, has not publicly commented on the summit, but analysts say Pyongyang may hope its allies will use the meeting to advance its longstanding demands for recognition as a nuclear-armed state and relief from international sanctions.
Competing nuclear interests
The United States and Russia have decades of experience negotiating nuclear arms control agreements, but China has resisted joining similar negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains substantially smaller.
Cheng said that China’s continued nuclear expansion and reliance on strategic deterrence would make a trilateral agreement difficult.
He said Washington would seek a commitment from Xi to restrain China’s nuclear arsenal, while Beijing and Moscow would pursue their own objectives in negotiations with Trump.
“All three have their own calculations, and they can’t work together,” Cheng said. “Under those circumstances, a joint statement would be meaningless.”
Spectators wave Chinese flags as military vehicles carrying DF-41 nuclear ballistic missiles roll during a parade to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the founding of Communist China in Beijing, Oct. 1, 2019.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) Xi will likely use the summit to demonstrate China’s status as a major power and strengthen his domestic political authority, Song Guocheng, a Taiwanese international relations scholar, told RFA Mandarin.
He also considered a concrete nuclear arms control agreement unlikely but said the leaders could still make progress on reducing nuclear risks.
The leaders “could establish what we call a nuclear weapons communication mechanism, with emergency procedures or arrangements between them,” Song said. “That could at least help prevent nuclear miscalculations.”
China’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that the leaders would exchange views on maintaining world peace and promoting strategic stability among major powers.
Beijing has previously said requiring China to participate in trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage would be neither reasonable nor realistic.
North Korea seeks recognition, fears concessions
For North Korea, analysts say the summit could provide an opportunity to seek diplomatic support for its nuclear ambitions, although Pyongyang is not participating in the talks.
North Korea likely hopes that China and Russia will convey Pyongyang’s demands to Trump, Kim Tae-woo, a former president of the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification, told RFA Korean.
“North Korea essentially has two demands and expectations when it comes to nuclear weapons,” Kim said. “The first is recognition of its status as a nuclear-armed state. The second is that any nuclear talks with the United States must be conducted as arms reduction negotiations between nuclear powers on an equal footing.”
Analysts said an explicit endorsement of North Korea’s nuclear status was unlikely, but the absence of calls for denuclearization could still be welcomed by Pyongyang.
This image distributed by the North Korean government on March 24, 2022, and not independently verifiable shows leader Kim Jong Un walking away from what state media reports as a "new type" of intercontinental ballistic missile.
(KCNA via Reuters) “North Korea will hope that there are no statements about stability on the Korean Peninsula or North Korea’s denuclearization,” Shin Beom-chul, South Korea’s former vice minister of national defense, told RFA Korean. “They will be satisfied as long as denuclearization is not discussed.”
North Korea may also hope Beijing and Moscow will press Washington to ease sanctions, analysts said.
In December 2017, the U.N. Security Council – which includes Russia and China – adopted Resolution 2397, which imposed tighter restrictions on North Korea’s petroleum supplies, exports and overseas workers.
The summit could present risks for Pyongyang if China or Russia uses their relationships with North Korea as leverage.
Recent high-level diplomatic exchanges between North Korea and its neighbors might be showing Pyongyang’s concerns about being sidelined, Ko Young-hwan, a former president of South Korea’s National Institute for Unification Education, told RFA Korean.
“The war in Ukraine won’t go on forever,” Ko said. “North Korea is probably worried that China and Russia might do something with the United States behind its back.”
South Korea’s presidential office has said Seoul’s position and interests must be fully reflected in discussions among the three powers.
Prospects for further talks
Beyond nuclear arms control, analysts differ on whether the summit could lead to a more permanent diplomatic framework among Washington, Beijing and Moscow.
A scholar of U.S.-China relations identified only as Mr. Xing told RFA Mandarin that the meeting could signal the emergence of a “new Yalta system,” referring to the 1945 conference at which Allied leaders discussed the postwar international order.
Members of the "Art Lift" collective carry the artwork showing U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping next to the 'Big Three' monument with the leaders at the 1945 Yalta conference - Joseph Stalin, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill, in Livadia park in Yalta, Crimea, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters) Xing predicted the summit would remain largely symbolic, with China unlikely to support a formal consultation mechanism.
The U.S.-based Arms Control Association said ahead of the meeting that a single summit was unlikely to produce a major breakthrough, but the leaders could instruct negotiating teams to begin sustained discussions on nuclear arms limits and risk reduction.
The Kremlin said the parties were discussing a possible joint communiqué. If they cannot agree on a text, the three leaders will issue separate assessments of the talks.
Edited by Taejun Kang and Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Govt to fund sub-degree progs
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau announced today that the Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors will subsidise 2,196 places in 35 sub-degree…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau announced today that the Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors will subsidise 2,196 places in 35 sub-degree programmes at five post-secondary institutions for the 2027/28 academic year.

The programmes span seven disciplines facing strong manpower demand: architecture and engineering, computer science, creative industries, healthcare, sports and recreation, testing and certification, and tourism and hospitality.

Annual subsidies for the 2027/28 academic year will be $40,730 for laboratory-based programmes and $23,390 for non-laboratory-based programmes.

The subsidy applies to both new and continuing eligible students and covers the normal duration of the programmes.

Students in need may still apply for assistance from the Student Finance Office under the Working Family & Student Financial Assistance Agency to help cover the remaining tuition fees payable.

articles.title: Smiles and hugs ahead of Trump, Xi and Putin’s highly anticipated meeting
articles.excerpt: Shenzhen – China’s tech capital – rolls out the red carpet for the 33rd APEC summit.
articles.fullText:
SHENZHEN, China – U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the bottom of the stairs of Air Force One upon landing in China on Wednesday for this week’s APEC summit.
Trump, Xi, Putin at APEC in Shenzhen
Both leaders embraced on the red carpet at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport as a crowd of women waved American flags and chanted “warm welcome” in Mandarin. Trump had just flown in from Manila where he had attended the ASEAN summit. The scene echoed Trump’s welcome at Joint Base Andrews at the start of Xi’s state visit to the United States in September.
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes U.S. President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China Nov. 18, 2026.
(Carlos Barria/Reuters) Shenzhen is hosting leaders from 21 Asia-Pacific economies during the two-day summit, but the scheduled meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday is the highly anticipated event.
The planned talks – to be held at Shenzhen’s lakeside Kylin Villa – echo the February 1945 summit of Britain’s Winston Churchill, the Soviet Union’s Joseph Stalin and U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in Yalta, months before the end of World War II.
“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters about the meeting last week.
Trump later arrived at the venue of the APEC dinner, pausing to enjoy a rendition of “America the Beautiful” by a Chinese string and woodwind ensemble before being greeted by Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan.
Servers prepare for a welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026.
(Maxim Shemetov/AFP) As leaders gathered for the APEC family photo ahead of the dinner, a smiling Putin walked up to Trump and extended his hand as Xi looked on.
At the dinner, Xi took the stage and offered a toast to the “shared prosperity” of the Asia-Pacific region.
Shenzhen sparkles
As host city to the 33rd meeting of APEC economic leaders, China’s tech capital was on full display Wednesday. Promotional signage adorned the airport, many buildings and roadways. Flags decorated the trees and lampposts, giving the entire city a festive atmosphere.
A woman walks past a decorative sign for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 16, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) The streets were pristine, with everything meticulously organized, as if the city was eager to showcase its rapid development.
At the same time, police were stationed throughout the city to control traffic and ensure security. A heavy police presence was also evident around the International Media Center, where journalists from across the globe had gathered.
To enter the center, journalists passed through security checkpoints and were subject to rigorous screening; their photographs automatically appeared on a screen as they underwent baggage inspections and body searches, reflecting a strict emphasis on security protocols.
Security agents guard the hotel where U.S. President Donald Trump will stay during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov 18, 2026.
(Pedro Pardo/AFP) Amid these measures, numerous volunteers were stationed on the shuttle buses connecting hotels to the media center, as well as inside the hotels and the media center itself, to assist journalists and other attendees.
The two-day summit ends Thursday, after which Trump is scheduled to immediately return to the U.S.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: What to know about Ring Drone Cam, which can patrol your home for $250
articles.excerpt: Ring's Drone Cam flies room to room with AI navigation, 2K video and a $249.99 price, but it still awaits…
articles.fullText:
Ever leave the house and suddenly wonder whether you closed the back door? You pull up your security camera, but it only shows the driveway. Not much help when you want to see what's happening inside. Well, Ring thinks it has an answer. And this one actually flies. Amazon-owned Ring has unveiled the Ring Drone Cam, a tiny $249.99 indoor security camera that flies from room to room. It can investigate security alerts, check specific areas of your home and send live video directly to your phone.
Earlier this month, the company announced the new drone as part of its new Ring Robotics lineup. And thanks to artificial intelligence , it can navigate your home without someone steering it around. We also talked in depth about this new technology on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast," including what a flying camera could mean for home security. But before you get too excited about having your own miniature security patrol, there are some things worth knowing.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams , find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI ROBOT MAY STOP YOUR DOG FROM BARKING WHILE YOU'RE GONE
Traditional home security cameras have one obvious limitation. They only show what's in front of them. Ring wants to change that. The Ring Drone Cam uses a system called AI Pilot to learn the layout of your home. During the initial setup, you carry the drone through your space while it creates a digital floor plan. From there, the system identifies rooms and suggests places worth checking. For example, maybe you want to see whether a window is open. Or perhaps your security system detects movement near the back door. You can save those locations in the Ring app. Then, when you want a closer look, the drone can fly there automatically. You can also create customized routes and schedule patrols with a compatible Ring subscription.
The drone can work with connected Ring cameras and security sensors . If a linked device triggers an alert, Ring Drone Cam can automatically fly to a previously selected location to investigate. According to Ring's official announcement, AI Pilot combines cameras with onboard sensors and cloud processing to navigate around obstacles. So, instead of wondering what triggered an alert, you could actually see what's happening in another part of the house.
The Ring Drone Cam weighs approximately 5.8 ounces and packs quite a bit of technology into its compact design. It records video at 1920 by 1920 resolution, which Ring describes as 2K. The camera has a 148-degree field of view and can rotate to capture a 360-degree view of a room. You can watch live footage through the Ring app. And if something happens at night, the drone has two built-in LED spotlights that illuminate dark areas. Unlike some traditional security cameras, it doesn't use infrared night vision. The drone also makes noise while flying. That's intentional. Ring says the audible propellers help people know when the camera is moving around.
The drone has no microphone or speaker, so you cannot hear what's happening or talk to someone through it. There's also no built-in siren. And although it can move independently, it doesn't stay airborne indefinitely. Ring advertises up to eight minutes of flight time on a fully charged battery under controlled conditions. When the flight ends or the battery runs low, the drone returns to its charging dock.
If this concept sounds familiar, there's a good reason. Ring originally announced a flying indoor security camera called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020. It was an ambitious idea at the time. Instead of installing cameras throughout your house, you could use one device to check different rooms. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff explained the thinking behind that original concept. In his September 2020 announcement, Siminoff wrote: "We wanted to create one camera that could give users the flexibility of every viewpoint they want around the home." However, bringing that concept to a broad consumer launch took much longer than expected.
More than six years later, Ring is returning to the idea with a new product called Ring Drone Cam. This version uses AI to map your home, navigate around obstacles and fly to specific locations through the Ring app. In the company's November 2026 announcement, Siminoff explained what customers had been asking for. "For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn't reach." The new drone reflects that feedback. Ring announced the original Always Home Cam at $249.99 in 2020. The new Ring Drone Cam carries that same advertised price in 2026. So, despite years of development and the addition of AI navigation, the announced price hasn't changed. That's pretty remarkable for a product with this kind of technology.
WHAT A SMART FIREWALL DOES AND WHY IT MATTERS ON HOME WI-FI
Ring says its AI Pilot system can recognize obstacles and adjust its flight path as it moves. However, certain surfaces can make navigation more difficult. According to Ring's official product information, highly reflective floors, large mirrors and transparent glass can interfere with navigation. Rooms with plain walls and few visual details may also create challenges.
The drone is limited to single-floor operation at launch, although Ring plans to support multiple floors in the future. It also requires Wi-Fi and a suitable location for its charging dock. Ring recommends an upload speed of at least 5 Mbps for optimal performance and 10 Mbps for 2K video quality.
Ring says it has built several privacy protections into the device. Ring says the new Drone Cam only records while flying. When it returns to its docking station, the camera stops recording and the device powers down. A visible indicator and audible propellers help let people know when the drone is operating. The company also says recordings will receive protection through its new Throw Away the Key encryption system, known as TAKE. According to Ring's privacy documentation, the company retains video encryption keys for up to 24 hours to support enabled features. It then deletes its copies of those keys, leaving customers with control of the keys needed to access their recordings.
However, TAKE differs from traditional end-to-end encryption because it allows Ring to process video for certain connected features during that initial period. There's another consideration. AI Pilot uses cloud processing as part of its navigation system. So, anyone thinking about buying one should understand how Ring handles the home's digital map and what information gets processed remotely. And if you share your home with someone else, it's worth discussing whether they're comfortable with a flying camera operating indoors .
Here's something else to keep in mind before deciding whether this little drone belongs in your home. The advertised price is $249.99. That includes the drone and its charging dock. However, some features require a compatible Ring subscription. For example, you need a subscription to schedule automatic patrols. You'll also need a compatible plan if you want to save recordings in the cloud and review them later.
Without a subscription, you can still use Live View to check what's happening. But if you want the drone to maintain a video history, there will be an additional recurring cost. Ring says eligible plans can provide up to 180 days of cloud video history, depending on the subscription and settings. And there's one more thing to consider. The drone relies on its battery for flight. With a maximum advertised flight time of eight minutes, you'll need to allow time for recharging between patrols. That makes it better suited for checking specific areas than watching your entire house continuously.
FLOCK CEO, TECH RIVALS CALLED TO TESTIFY BEFORE SENATORS OVER AI CAMERA PRIVACY CONCERNS
Ring says the Drone Cam is scheduled to begin shipping in the U.S. on January 27, 2027. The announced price is $249.99. However, the company still needs authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.
So far, Ring says the device has not received the required FCC authorization and cannot legally be offered for sale or lease until that approval arrives. For now, you can sign up for product availability updates through Ring's official website at ring.com/products/drone-cam . And if you're wondering whether it will actually fly around your house as smoothly as it does in promotional videos, that's something we'll have to evaluate when the product becomes available.
I have to say, I love the idea of a security camera that can actually fly through your home. If I'm away and something triggers an alert, I'd much rather send a camera to check it out than wonder what's happening beyond the view of my existing cameras. And at $250, Ring has certainly priced this to get people's attention. What I'm curious about is how well it actually flies through a home. Can it navigate doorways and avoid obstacles reliably? And then there's the privacy question. I'd want to know exactly how Ring handles the map of my home and who can access the footage. I'm looking forward to seeing this technology in action.
We also talked about it in depth on my podcast, The CyberGuy Report at cyberguy.com/podcast . Check it out and subscribe for more conversations about the latest technology changing our lives.
Would you let an AI-powered drone fly through your house to keep an eye on things, or would a camera that can roam from room to room feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
